lessons.title: Linear first-order equations and models
lessons.summary: Turn the left-hand side into one product derivative.
lessons.objective: Use an integrating factor, apply the initial condition and identify the solution interval.
lessons.before: Review the product and chain rules, separable equations and integration techniques. Logarithmic, trigonometric and hyperbolic factors may require earlier Pure Mathematics identities.
lessons.ideas:
Divide into standard form first

A linear first-order equation can be written as \(y^{\prime}+P(x)y=Q(x)\) on an interval where its leading coefficient is non-zero. The coefficient of y′ must be 1 before identifying P. A non-zero integrating factor converts the left side into a product derivative.

\[\begin{gathered}\mu=e^{\int P(x)\,dx},\qquad\frac{\mu^{\prime}}\mu=P\\(\mu y)^{\prime}=\mu Q\\y=\frac{\int\mu Q\,dx+C}{\mu}\end{gathered}\]

One multiplicative constant in μ is unnecessary; it is absorbed into C. Integrate first, then apply the initial condition to the whole solution. A constant must not be placed in a different part of the expression when dividing by μ.

The interval belongs to the original equation

Record forbidden points from the original leading coefficient and denominators. A cancelled factor does not restore a point where the original equation is undefined. Use a connected interval containing the initial point. For logarithms, use absolute values when required; remove them only after fixing a branch on that interval.

Exceptional parameter values

A general parameter formula may divide by zero at a special value. Solve the equation at that value directly instead of discarding the case. An exponential forcing with the same rate as the homogeneous solution can produce a factor x.

Build a model from rates

For a well-mixed tank, mass change equals mass entering per unit time minus mass leaving per unit time. The outgoing concentration is current mass divided by current volume. State constant-volume and mixing assumptions. Distinguish mass, concentration and time units.

A periodic approximation is not a limit

A decaying transient may leave a non-constant oscillation. The difference from that oscillation tends to zero, while the function itself has no finite pointwise limit.
lessons.method:
1. Specify the real interval and divide by the leading coefficient.
  2. Identify P and construct a non-zero integrating factor.
  3. Integrate the product derivative and keep one arbitrary constant.
  4. Apply the initial condition and recover the original dependent variable.
  5. Check the equation, interval, model units and any exceptional parameter value.
mistakes: Divide the whole equation, not only the y′ term.
The integrating factor uses P after standardisation.
Keep C inside the numerator when dividing by μ.
Cancelling a factor does not repair a singularity of the original equation.
A periodic long-term response is not a constant limit.

examples.title: 1 · A polynomial input
examples.question: Solve \(y^{\prime}+3y=6x-1\), with \(y(0)=2\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mu=e^{3x},\qquad(e^{3x}y)^{\prime}=(6x-1)e^{3x}\\e^{3x}y=(2x-1)e^{3x}+C\\C=3,\qquad y=2x-1+3e^{-3x}\end{gathered}\]

The final exponential term satisfies the homogeneous equation; differentiating the whole result verifies both the input and the initial value.

examples.title: 2 · Keep the original interval
examples.question: For x>0, solve \(y^{\prime}+\frac2x y=x^2\), with \(y(1)=2\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mu=x^2,\qquad(x^2y)^{\prime}=x^4\\x^2y=\frac{x^5}{5}+C,\qquad C=\frac95\\y=\frac{x^3}{5}+\frac9{5x^2}\end{gathered}\]

The equation is undefined at zero. The solution to this initial-value problem is considered on x>0, even though the algebraic formula can also be evaluated on a separate negative interval.

examples.title: 3 · Solve the exceptional case separately
examples.question: Solve \(y^{\prime}+ky=3e^{-x}\), \(y(0)=2\), distinguishing k=1.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}k\ne1:\quad y=\frac3{k-1}e^{-x}\\\quad+\left(2-\frac3{k-1}\right)e^{-kx}\\k=1:\quad(e^xy)^{\prime}=3\\y=(2+3x)e^{-x}\end{gathered}\]

The second formula is obtained from the original equation at k=1. For k>0 both cases tend to zero, including the polynomial-times-exponential term.

examples.title: 4 · Mass and concentration are different quantities
examples.question: A well-mixed tank holds 20 litres. It initially contains 10 grams of salt. Liquid containing 2 grams per litre enters at 1 litre per minute and leaves at the same rate. Find the concentration and when it first reaches 1.5 grams per litre.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}S^{\prime}=2-\frac S{20},\qquad S(0)=10\\S=40-30e^{-t/20}\\c=\frac S{20}=2-\frac32e^{-t/20}\\c=\frac32\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=20\ln3\end{gathered}\]

The outgoing mass rate is \(\frac S{20}\) grams per minute. The concentration increases from 0.5 towards 2, so the stated crossing is unique.

lessons.title: Complementary functions and initial conditions
lessons.summary: Choose the correct two-constant form for the auxiliary roots.
lessons.objective: Construct second-order solutions and apply both conditions to the complete function.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Work on the stated real interval and retain exact values.

Review complex powers for the real form arising from conjugate auxiliary roots.
lessons.ideas:
Start with the homogeneous equation

For constant coefficients, try an exponential in \(ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=0\). Its non-zero factor leaves the auxiliary equation. The leading coefficient a must be non-zero.

\[\begin{gathered}a\lambda^2+b\lambda+c=0\\\lambda_1\ne\lambda_2\text{ real}:\quad y_{\rm CF}=Ae^{\lambda_1x}+Be^{\lambda_2x}\\\lambda\text{ repeated}:\quad y_{\rm CF}=(A+Bx)e^{\lambda x}\\\alpha\pm i\beta:\quad y_{\rm CF}=e^{\alpha x}(A\cos\beta x+B\sin\beta x)\end{gathered}\]

For the conjugate-root form take β>0. Two copies of the same exponential are not independent; that is why a repeated root needs the factor x. Each arbitrary constant belongs to the complementary function.

Add a particular integral for the actual input

If L(y) denotes ay′′+by′+cy and L(p)=f, then L(yCF+p)=f by linearity. A particular integral is one fixed function with no new arbitrary constants. It need not satisfy the initial conditions by itself.

A first polynomial trial

When the input is quadratic and c≠0, try \(p=Ux^2+Vx+W\). Substitution gives a triangular coefficient system.

\[\begin{gathered}L(p)=cUx^2+(2bU+cV)x\\\quad+(2aU+bV+cW)\end{gathered}\]

Match every coefficient with the given input, then add the complementary function. The next lesson develops these trials further.

Use the conditions on the whole solution

Differentiate the complete yCF+p before substituting. In a conjugate-root form the derivative includes the exponential factor as well as the trigonometric derivatives. Two independent conditions determine the two constants; check the resulting values in both conditions.

Reading the homogeneous modes

Negative real parts give decaying homogeneous terms. A zero real part can give persistent oscillation, and a positive real part allows growth. Repeated negative roots still decay despite the polynomial factor. Examine the actual constants before declaring that a growing mode is present.
lessons.method:
1. Form the auxiliary equation and find its root type.
  2. Write two independent homogeneous modes.
  3. Find or verify a particular integral for a non-zero input.
  4. Apply both conditions to the complete solution and its derivative.
  5. Substitute back and interpret the actual modes.
mistakes: A repeated root needs x times the exponential as its second mode.
Use both real and imaginary parts of a conjugate-root pair correctly.
Differentiate the exponential factor as well as sine and cosine.
Initial conditions apply to CF plus PI, not CF alone.
A positive auxiliary root permits growth but its coefficient may vanish.

examples.title: 1 · Two distinct real modes
examples.question: Solve \(y^{\prime\prime}+y^{\prime}-6y=0\), \(y(0)=3\) and \(y^{\prime}(0)=1\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}(\lambda-2)(\lambda+3)=0\\y=Ae^{2x}+Be^{-3x}\\A+B=3,\qquad2A-3B=1\\A=2,\quad B=1,\qquad y=2e^{2x}+e^{-3x}\end{gathered}\]

The two rates are different, giving two independent modes. The positive-rate term is present for these particular conditions.

examples.title: 2 · A repeated auxiliary root
examples.question: Solve \(y^{\prime\prime}+4y^{\prime}+4y=0\), \(y(0)=1\) and \(y^{\prime}(0)=3\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}(\lambda+2)^2=0\\y=(A+Bx)e^{-2x}\\A=1,\qquad B-2A=3\\y=(1+5x)e^{-2x}\end{gathered}\]

The solution decays as x increases, although its initial gradient is positive. Initial direction and long-term behaviour are different questions.

examples.title: 3 · Real form from complex roots
examples.question: Solve \(y^{\prime\prime}+2y^{\prime}+10y=0\), \(y(0)=2\) and \(y^{\prime}(0)=1\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\lambda=-1\pm3i\\y=e^{-x}(A\cos3x+B\sin3x)\\A=2,\qquad-A+3B=1\\y=e^{-x}(2\cos3x+\sin3x)\end{gathered}\]

The coefficient of \(\sin3x\) is 1, after the factor 3 in its derivative is included.

examples.title: 4 · The conditions apply to CF plus PI
examples.question: For \(y^{\prime\prime}+2y^{\prime}+5y=5x^2+4x-3\), verify \(p=x^2-1\) is a particular integral and find the solution with y(0)=\(y^{\prime}(0)=0\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}L(x^2-1)=2+4x+5(x^2-1)\\=5x^2+4x-3\\y=x^2-1+e^{-x}(A\cos2x+B\sin2x)\\A=1,\qquad-A+2B=0\\y=x^2-1+e^{-x}\left(\cos2x+\frac12\sin2x\right)\end{gathered}\]

Using yCF(0)=0 instead would miss the −1 contributed by the particular integral.

lessons.title: Polynomial and exponential particular integrals
lessons.summary: Find the input response before fitting the homogeneous constants.
lessons.objective: Use suitable trials and superposition, then check the complete initial-value solution.
lessons.before: Complete the preceding lesson. Work on the stated real interval and retain exact values.
lessons.ideas:
Keep CF and PI separate while working

The complementary function solves the zero-input equation. A particular integral produces the specified right-hand side. If the equation is linear, the sum of particular integrals for separate inputs produces the sum of those inputs.

Polynomial inputs need all lower powers

For a quadratic input use \(Ux^2+Vx+W\) when appropriate, including lower powers even if one is absent from the input. Differentiation mixes degrees. If the usual trial duplicates a homogeneous mode, a modified or supplied form is needed; the next lesson treats the stated resonant examples.

Exponential inputs

\[\begin{gathered}L(Ke^{kx})=K(ak^2+bk+c)e^{kx}\\K=\frac{F}{ak^2+bk+c}\quad\text{if the denominator is non-zero}\end{gathered}\]

This formula follows by differentiating the trial twice, not by replacing the derivatives with the input itself. The denominator being zero means the trial cannot produce a non-zero input; it does not mean that the differential equation has no solution.

Superpose, then use the initial conditions

For polynomial plus exponential forcing, add the two verified particular responses. Differentiate that entire expression before finding the complementary constants. A particular integral may be rewritten by adding a homogeneous term; what matters is the complete family and satisfaction of the original equation.

Parameters can remove a mode

When a free initial slope controls the coefficient of a growing exponential, solve for the slope that makes that coefficient zero. The remaining solution can still grow because of a polynomial input. Distinguish a finite limit, a polynomial approximation and a vanishing transient.
lessons.method:
1. Find the complementary function once.
  2. Choose a trial containing every required polynomial term or the correct exponential rate.
  3. Differentiate and match coefficients with the input.
  4. Combine inputs by addition, then apply the initial conditions to the whole function.
  5. Check the residual and classify the surviving long-term terms.
mistakes: A quadratic trial usually needs constant and linear terms too.
A trial duplicating a CF mode cannot produce a non-zero input.
Superposition adds responses; it does not multiply them.
The PI generally does not satisfy the initial conditions alone.
Removing an unstable mode does not necessarily give a constant limit.

examples.title: 1 · Match the whole quadratic
examples.question: Solve \(y^{\prime\prime}+3y^{\prime}+2y=2x^2+2x+2\), \(y(0)=1\) and \(y^{\prime}(0)=0\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}p=Ux^2+Vx+W\\2U=2,\quad6U+2V=2,\quad2U+3V+2W=2\\p=x^2-2x+3\\y=Ae^{-x}+Be^{-2x}+p\\A=-2,\quad B=0\\y=x^2-2x+3-2e^{-x}\end{gathered}\]

Both constants are solved, even though one turns out to be zero.

examples.title: 2 · A non-resonant exponential input
examples.question: Find the general solution of \(y^{\prime\prime}-y^{\prime}-2y=12e^{3x}\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\lambda=2,-1,\qquad p=Ke^{3x}\\(9-3-2)K=12,\qquad K=3\\y=Ae^{2x}+Be^{-x}+3e^{3x}\end{gathered}\]

The trial is independent of both complementary modes, so no extra polynomial factor is needed.

examples.title: 3 · Add responses for two inputs
examples.question: Find the general solution of \(y^{\prime\prime}+3y^{\prime}+2y=2x+7+6e^x\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}L(x+2)=2x+7,\qquad L(e^x)=6e^x\\p=x+2+e^x\\y=Ae^{-x}+Be^{-2x}+x+2+e^x\end{gathered}\]

The displayed PI is the sum of two independently verified responses. The complementary function is included once.

examples.title: 4 · Choose an initial slope to suppress growth
examples.question: For \(y^{\prime\prime}-y^{\prime}-2y=-2x\), keep \(y(0)=1\) and choose y′(0)=v so that the growing exponential is absent.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}p=x-\frac12\\y=Ae^{2x}+Be^{-x}+x-\frac12\\A+B=\frac32,\qquad2A-B+1=v\\A=\frac{2v+1}{6}\\v=-\frac12,\qquad y=\frac32e^{-x}+x-\frac12\end{gathered}\]

The remaining solution still grows linearly. Its difference from \(x-\frac12\) tends to zero; y itself has no finite limit.

lessons.title: Oscillatory forcing, resonance and long-term behaviour
lessons.summary: Distinguish a periodic response from its transient.
lessons.objective: Find harmonic responses and use supplied resonant trial forms with the correct initial data.
lessons.before: Complete the preceding lesson. Work on the stated real interval and retain exact values.
lessons.ideas:
Use both sine and cosine in the trial

For a sine, cosine or mixed input of frequency ω, try p=\(U\sin(\omega x)+V\cos(\omega x)\) when appropriate. The first derivative mixes the two functions, even if the input contains only one of them.

\[\begin{gathered}L(p)=\bigl((c-a\omega^2)U-b\omega V\bigr)\sin\omega x\\\quad+\bigl(b\omega U+(c-a\omega^2)V\bigr)\cos\omega x\end{gathered}\]

Match the sine and cosine coefficients separately. After finding the PI, include the CF and apply the conditions to the entire expression.

Amplitude and phase need a convention

For \(U\sin(\omega x)+V\cos(\omega x)\), the amplitude is \(\sqrt{U^2+V^2}\). In \(R\sin(\omega x+\phi)\), use \(R\cos\phi=U\) and \(R\sin\phi=V\). The signs fix the quadrant; a tangent ratio alone does not. A cosine-based phase convention has different coefficient equations.

When the trial overlaps a homogeneous mode

A resonant input can make a usual exponential or harmonic trial disappear under L. In the written resonant tasks, the modified trial is supplied. Differentiate that given form and determine its coefficient by substitution. A repeated auxiliary root can require a squared polynomial factor rather than a single x.

State the actual large-time conclusion

If every CF mode decays, its difference from the particular response tends to zero. A non-constant periodic response still has no finite pointwise limit. If a growing CF mode has a non-zero coefficient, the periodic PI need not approximate the solution. Always inspect the actual constants and real parts.
lessons.method:
1. Choose both harmonic terms or use the supplied resonant trial.
  2. Differentiate the complete trial and match the input coefficients.
  3. Add the complementary function and use both conditions.
  4. Choose the phase quadrant from both sine and cosine coefficients.
  5. Prove that the transient vanishes before claiming a long-term approximation.
mistakes: A pure cosine input can still need a sine term in the PI.
Keep the frequency factors in both derivatives.
A resonant trial has to be tested, not assigned a zero denominator.
The signs of two coefficients determine the phase quadrant.
An asymptotic periodic response does not imply a pointwise limit.

examples.title: 1 · A periodic response after decay
examples.question: Solve \(y^{\prime\prime}+2y^{\prime}+5y=20\cos x\), y(0)=\(y^{\prime}(0)=0\), and describe the long-term response.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}p=U\sin x+V\cos x\\4U-2V=0,\qquad2U+4V=20\\U=2,\quad V=4\\y=2\sin x+4\cos x\\\quad-e^{-x}(4\cos2x+3\sin2x)\end{gathered}\]

The difference from \(2\sin x+4\cos x=2\sqrt5\cos(x-\phi)\), with \(\tan\phi=1/2\) in the first quadrant, tends to zero. The solution has no finite pointwise limit.

examples.title: 2 · A PI that does not dominate
examples.question: For \(y^{\prime\prime}-2y^{\prime}+2y=5\sin x+5\cos x\), \(y(0)=4\) and \(y^{\prime}(0)=0\), is the periodic PI a large-x approximation?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}p=-\sin x+3\cos x\\y=e^x\cos x-\sin x+3\cos x\end{gathered}\]

No. The difference from p is \(e^x\cos x\), which does not tend to zero. Its values along full turns grow without bound, even though the difference vanishes at some other arguments.

examples.title: 3 · Test a supplied resonant form
examples.question: For \(y^{\prime\prime}+y^{\prime}-2y=4e^x\), use the supplied trial \(p=Kxe^x\) and give the general solution.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}L(Kxe^x)=3Ke^x\\K=\frac43\\y=Ae^x+Be^{-2x}+\frac43xe^x\end{gathered}\]

The ordinary exponential trial duplicates a CF mode. The supplied extra x makes a non-zero input possible.

examples.title: 4 · A repeated resonant root
examples.question: For \(y^{\prime\prime}+6y^{\prime}+9y=8e^{-3x}\), use \(p=Kx^2e^{-3x}\). Find the solution with \(y(0)=2\) and \(y^{\prime}(0)=1\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}L(Kx^2e^{-3x})=2Ke^{-3x}\\K=4,\qquad y=(A+Bx+4x^2)e^{-3x}\\A=2,\qquad B-3A=1\\y=(2+7x+4x^2)e^{-3x}\end{gathered}\]

The complete solution tends to zero. A fixed polynomial times a decaying exponential still decays.

lessons.title: Substitutions, real branches and transformed conditions
lessons.summary: Transform the derivatives and data before solving the simpler equation.
lessons.objective: Use the given dependent or independent variable substitution and recover the correct real solution.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Work on the stated real interval and retain exact values.

Review the chain rule twice and inverse hyperbolic functions. Some reduced first-order equations are separable.
lessons.ideas:
Differentiate the given substitution explicitly

For \(v=g(x)y\), apply the product rule twice. For \(v=\phi(y)\), apply the chain rule twice. These are different operations.

\[\begin{gathered}v=gy:\quad v^{\prime}=g^{\prime}y+gy^{\prime}\\v^{\prime\prime}=g^{\prime\prime}y+2g^{\prime}y^{\prime}+gy^{\prime\prime}\\v=\phi(y):\quad v^{\prime}=\phi^{\prime}(y)y^{\prime}\\v^{\prime\prime}=\phi^{\prime\prime}(y)(y^{\prime})^2+\phi^{\prime}(y)y^{\prime\prime}\end{gathered}\]

Substitute these expressions into the original relation. Simplify before dividing, and record any factor required to be non-zero. Initial derivatives change too; for v=gy use \(v^{\prime}(x_0)=g^{\prime}(x_0)y(x_0)+g(x_0)y^{\prime}(x_0)\).

A change of independent variable has two chain factors

For \(x=e^u\), write \(u=\ln x\) and work on x>0.

\[\begin{gathered}xy_x=y_u,\qquad x^2y_{xx}=y_{uu}-y_u\end{gathered}\]

The negative first-derivative term comes from differentiating 1/x. The final answer must return to x, with the original initial data and domain.

First-order substitutions and separation

For \(y=xv\), use \(y^{\prime}=v+xv^{\prime}\). An affine combination \(z=ax+by\) has derivative \(z^{\prime}=a+by^{\prime}\). After the given substitution, solve the resulting separable or linear equation. Dividing by a function of the new variable may exclude a constant solution; check it in the original equation.

Recover the specified real branch

A reciprocal needs a non-zero denominator. A positive square or fourth-root solution uses the positive root. A real cube root can be negative, but the recovered function must still have the differentiability required by the original equation. For the cubic substitution in Q69, a formal zero of v does not give permission to pass through y=0.

Domain proof is part of the solution

Check a radical stays non-negative, a logarithm has positive input, and any denominator stays non-zero on the proposed interval. A bound such as a positive quadratic minimum minus a decaying oscillation amplitude can establish global positivity.
lessons.method:
1. Write the substitution and all required first and second derivatives.
  2. Transform the initial values and derivative data at the correct point.
  3. Solve the reduced equation while recording excluded cases.
  4. Recover the original variable using the required real branch.
  5. Check the original equation, conditions, differentiability and interval.
mistakes: A second chain derivative generally has two terms.
Initial derivative data also change under a substitution.
A reciprocal substitution can exclude the zero solution.
Choose the stated real branch rather than adding an unrelated sign.
A formal inverse formula must still satisfy the original domain and smoothness.

examples.title: 1 · A product removes variable coefficients
examples.question: For x>0, use v=xy to solve \(xy^{\prime\prime}+(2+3x)y^{\prime}+(3+2x)y=2x+3\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v^{\prime}=y+xy^{\prime},\qquad v^{\prime\prime}=2y^{\prime}+xy^{\prime\prime}\\v^{\prime\prime}+3v^{\prime}+2v=2x+3\\v=Ae^{-x}+Be^{-2x}+x\\y=1+\frac{Ae^{-x}+Be^{-2x}}x\end{gathered}\]

The division by x is valid only on the stated interval. Substitution into the original variable-coefficient equation checks the recovery.

examples.title: 2 · Reciprocal substitution and an excluded solution
examples.question: Solve \(y^{\prime}+y=2y^2\), \(y(0)=\frac{1}{3}\), using \(v=\frac1y\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v^{\prime}=-\frac{y^{\prime}}{y^2}\\v^{\prime}-v=-2,\qquad v(0)=3\\v=2+e^x,\qquad y=\frac1{2+e^x}\end{gathered}\]

The denominator is positive for every real x. The original equation also has y=0 as a constant solution, but it does not satisfy this initial condition and is outside the reciprocal substitution.

examples.title: 3 · Change the independent variable
examples.question: For x>0, solve \(x^2y^{\prime\prime}+3xy^{\prime}+5y=10\ln x+4\), y(1)=\(y^{\prime}(1)=1\), using \(u=\ln x\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}y_{uu}+2y_u+5y=10u+4\\y(0)=1,\qquad y_u(0)=1\\y=2u+e^{-u}(A\cos2u+B\sin2u)\\A=1,\qquad B=0\\y=2\ln x+\frac{\cos(2\ln x)}x\end{gathered}\]

The derivative relation \(xy_x=y_u\) transforms the initial slope. Returning to x retains the restriction x>0.

examples.title: 4 · Recover only the positive square root
examples.question: A positive function satisfies \(yy^{\prime\prime}+(y^{\prime})^2+2yy^{\prime}+\frac52y^2=5e^{-x}\), \(y(0)=1\) and \(y^{\prime}(0)=- \frac{1}{2}\). Use \(v=y^2\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v^{\prime}=2yy^{\prime},\qquad v^{\prime\prime}=2(y^{\prime})^2+2yy^{\prime\prime}\\v^{\prime\prime}+2v^{\prime}+5v=10e^{-x}\\v=e^{-x}\left(\frac52-\frac32\cos2x\right)\\y=\sqrt{\frac{(5-3\cos2x)e^{-x}}2}\end{gathered}\]

The bracket in v is at least 1, so v is positive for every real x. The positive square root satisfies the stated condition; the negative branch does not. Its bounded oscillating factor times \(e^{-x}\) tends to zero, so y also tends to zero.

questions.title: A rational integrating factor
questions.prompt_html:
A differentiable function satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{2 x + 8}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}\,y=6\]

and \(y(0)=2\).

  1. Find the particular solution in exact logarithmic form.

    [8]

  2. State the maximal open interval containing \(x=0\) on which the equation and this solution are defined.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\left(\frac{3 \ln{\left(\frac{3 x + 6}{x + 6} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{6}\right) \left(x^{2} + 8 x + 12\right)\]

(b)

\[x\gt -2.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{2 x + 8}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}\,y=6\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{- 2 x - 8}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}\,\mathrm d x\right)=\frac{1}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\frac{6}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}.\]

Factor the quadratic and use partial fractions:

\[\frac6{(x+2)(x+6)}=\frac{3}{2(x+2)}-\frac{3}{2(x+6)}.\]
\[\mu y=\frac{3 \ln{\left(\frac{x + 2}{x + 6} \right)}}{2}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[\frac{1}{6}=- \frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}+C,\qquad C=\frac{1}{6} + \frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\left(x^{2} + 8 x + 12\right) \left(\frac{3 \ln{\left(\frac{x + 2}{x + 6} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{6} + \frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}\right).\]

On the interval containing the initial point the logarithms combine to give

\[y=\left(\frac{3 \ln{\left(\frac{3 x + 6}{x + 6} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{6}\right) \left(x^{2} + 8 x + 12\right).\]

(b)

The coefficient is undefined at \(x=-6,-2\). The connected interval containing zero is \((-2,\infty)\); there the logarithm argument is positive.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The numerator of the coefficient of \(y\) is the derivative of the quadratic denominator.

(b)

Do not cross a zero of the coefficient denominator.

marking_criteria.description_html: Recognise the linear form and find the reciprocal-quadratic integrating factor.
Form a product derivative and decompose the right side into partial fractions.
Integrate with the correct logarithmic coefficients.
Use the initial condition.
Give the exact explicit solution.

Required result and conditions:

\[x\gt -2.\]

questions.title: Completing the square inside an integrating factor
questions.prompt_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{x - 2}{x^{2} - 4 x + 13}\,y=2\]

with \(y(6)=5\).

  1. Find \(y\) in exact logarithmic form.

    [9]

  2. Explain why the formula is real for every real \(x\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9} \left(2 \ln{\left(\frac{x}{9} + \frac{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}}{9} - \frac{2}{9} \right)} + 1\right)\]

(b)

The square root is always positive and \(x-2+\sqrt{(x-2)^2+9}\gt 0\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{x - 2}{x^{2} - 4 x + 13}\,y=2\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{2 - x}{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}\,\mathrm d x\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}}.\]

Complete the square and use the inverse hyperbolic sine integral:

\[\int\frac{2}{\sqrt{(x-2)^2+9}}\,\mathrm dx=2\sinh^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{3}\right).\]
\[\mu y=2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \right)}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[1=2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{3} \right)}+C,\qquad C=1 - 2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{3} \right)}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9} \left(2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \right)} - 2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{3} \right)} + 1\right).\]

Since \(\sinh^{-1}(4/3)=\ln3\), use the logarithmic form of inverse hyperbolic sine:

\[y=\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9} \left(2 \ln{\left(\frac{x}{9} + \frac{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}}{9} - \frac{2}{9} \right)} + 1\right).\]

(b)

Because \(\sqrt{(x-2)^2+9}\gt |x-2|\), the numerator inside the logarithm is strictly positive, even when \(x\lt 2\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \((x-2)^2+3^2\) and an integrating factor proportional to its reciprocal square root.

(b)

Compare the square root with \(|x-2|\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the reciprocal-square-root integrating factor.
Obtain the correct product derivative.
Integrate using inverse hyperbolic sine.
Evaluate the constant and convert to logarithmic form.
Give a correctly scaled explicit expression for y.

Required result and conditions:

The square root is always positive and \(x-2+\sqrt{(x-2)^2+9}\gt 0\).

questions.title: Choosing the other radical factor
questions.prompt_html:
Consider the equation

\[\sqrt{x^{2} + 9}\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -y=x \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}\]

with \(y(4)=2\).

  1. Show that \(\sqrt{x^2+9}-x\) is an integrating factor after the equation has been put in linear form.

    [3]

  2. Hence find the particular solution.

    [6]

  3. Explain why division by this integrating factor is valid for all real \(x\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mu=\sqrt{x^2+9}-x.\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{- \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{\left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - \frac{55}{3}}{- x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}\]

(c)

\(\mu\gt 0\) for every real \(x\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Dividing by the square root gives \(P(x)=-1/\sqrt{x^2+9}\). If \(\mu=\sqrt{x^2+9}-x\), then

\[\mu^\prime=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+9}}-1=-\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{x^2+9}}.\]

Thus \(\mu^\prime/\mu=P\), as required.

(b)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}\,y=x\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int - \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}\,\mathrm d x\right)=- x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=x \left(- x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}\right).\]

After multiplication the right side is \(x\sqrt{x^2+9}-x^2\). Use \(u=x^2+9\) for the radical term.

\[\mu y=- \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{\left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[2=\frac{61}{3}+C,\qquad C=- \frac{55}{3}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{- \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{\left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - \frac{55}{3}}{- x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}.\]

(c)

\(\sqrt{x^2+9}\gt |x|\), so \(\sqrt{x^2+9}-x\gt 0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

It is enough to check \(\mu^\prime=P\mu\).

(b)

Integrate \(x\sqrt{x^2+9}-x^2\) before applying \(x=4\).

(c)

Use the positive square root.

marking_criteria.description_html:
Method and reasoning:

It is enough to check \(\mu^\prime=P\mu\).

Required result and conditions:

\[\mu=\sqrt{x^2+9}-x.\]

Method and reasoning:

Integrate \(x\sqrt{x^2+9}-x^2\) before applying \(x=4\).

Required result and conditions:

\[y=\frac{- \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{\left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - \frac{55}{3}}{- x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}\]

Required result and conditions:

\(\mu\gt 0\) for every real \(x\).

questions.title: A periodic input with a decaying response
questions.prompt_html:
Solve the initial-value problem

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +2\,y=- \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\]
\[y(0)=2.\]

  1. Use an integrating factor to find \(y\) explicitly.

    [7]

  2. Does \(y\) tend to a finite limit as \(x\to\infty\)? Justify your answer.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{\sin{\left(2 x \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + e^{- 2 x}\]

(b)

No. It approaches a periodic function, not a constant.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +2\,y=- \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int 2\,\mathrm d x\right)=e^{2 x}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\left(- \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right) e^{2 x}.\]

Integrate the exponential–trigonometric expression by parts twice, or differentiate the proposed antiderivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left[e^{2x}\left(\cos2x+\tfrac12\sin2x\right)\right]=e^{2x}(3\cos2x-\sin2x).\]
\[\mu y=\left(\frac{\sin{\left(2 x \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right) e^{2 x}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[2=1+C,\qquad C=1.\]

Therefore

\[y=\left(\left(\frac{\sin{\left(2 x \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right) e^{2 x} + 1\right) e^{- 2 x}.\]

(b)

The exponential term tends to zero. At \(x=n\pi\) the limiting values are \(1\), whereas at \(x=n\pi+\pi/2\) they are \(-1\). Hence a single limit does not exist.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The antiderivative of \(e^{2x}(3\cos2x-\sin2x)\) has the form \(e^{2x}(a\cos2x+b\sin2x)\).

(b)

Decay of the transient term does not make a nonconstant periodic term converge.

marking_criteria.description_html:
Method and reasoning:

The antiderivative of \(e^{2x}(3\cos2x-\sin2x)\) has the form \(e^{2x}(a\cos2x+b\sin2x)\).

Required result and conditions:

\[y=\frac{\sin{\left(2 x \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + e^{- 2 x}\]

Method and reasoning:

Decay of the transient term does not make a nonconstant periodic term converge.

Required result and conditions:

No. It approaches a periodic function, not a constant.

questions.title: Two partial-fraction steps
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\gt 0\),

\[\left(x^{2} + 4 x\right)\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +4\,y=2 x\]

and \(y(2)=1\).

  1. Find the particular solution in the form \(y=f(x)\).

    [9]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=-1 + \frac{\left(2 x + 8\right) \ln{\left(\frac{x}{6} + \frac{2}{3} \right)}}{x} + \frac{4}{x}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{4}{x^{2} + 4 x}\,y=\frac{2}{x + 4}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{4}{x \left(x + 4\right)}\,\mathrm d x\right)=\frac{x}{x + 4}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\frac{2 x}{\left(x + 4\right)^{2}}.\]

Use

\[\frac4{x(x+4)}=\frac1x-\frac1{x+4},\qquad \frac{2x}{(x+4)^2}=\frac2{x+4}-\frac8{(x+4)^2}.\]
\[\mu y=2 \ln{\left(x + 4 \right)} + \frac{8}{x + 4}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[\frac{1}{3}=\frac{4}{3} + \ln{\left(36 \right)}+C,\qquad C=- \ln{\left(36 \right)} - 1.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{\left(x + 4\right) \left(2 \ln{\left(x + 4 \right)} - \ln{\left(36 \right)} - 1 + \frac{8}{x + 4}\right)}{x}.\]

An equivalent simplified form is

\[y=-1 + \frac{\left(2 x + 8\right) \ln{\left(\frac{x}{6} + \frac{2}{3} \right)}}{x} + \frac{4}{x}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use partial fractions both for the integrating factor and for the resulting integral.

questions.title: A time-dependent rational coefficient
questions.prompt_html:
For \(t\gt 2/3\), the function \(x(t)\) satisfies

\[\left(9 t^{2} - 4\right)\,\frac{\mathrm d x}{\mathrm d t} +12\,x=18 t^{2} - 8\]

and \(x(1)=5\).

  1. Find \(x\) as an exact function of \(t\).

    [9]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[x=\frac{\left(3 t + 2\right) \left(2 t + \frac{8 \ln{\left(\frac{5}{3 t + 2} \right)}}{3} - 1\right)}{3 t - 2}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d x}{\mathrm d t} +\frac{12}{9 t^{2} - 4}\,x=2\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(t)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{12}{9 t^{2} - 4}\,\mathrm d t\right)=\frac{3 t - 2}{3 t + 2}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d t}\left(\mu x\right)=\frac{2 \left(3 t - 2\right)}{3 t + 2}.\]

The coefficient splits as

\[\frac{12}{9t^2-4}=\frac3{3t-2}-\frac3{3t+2}.\]

For the final integral use \(2(3t-2)/(3t+2)=2-8/(3t+2)\).

\[\mu x=2 t - \frac{8 \ln{\left(3 t + 2 \right)}}{3}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[1=2 - \frac{8 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}+C,\qquad C=-1 + \frac{8 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}.\]

Therefore

\[x=\frac{\left(3 t + 2\right) \left(2 t - \frac{8 \ln{\left(3 t + 2 \right)}}{3} - 1 + \frac{8 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}\right)}{3 t - 2}.\]
\[x=\frac{\left(3 t + 2\right) \left(2 t + \frac{8 \ln{\left(\frac{5}{3 t + 2} \right)}}{3} - 1\right)}{3 t - 2}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the factor 3 when integrating \((3t\pm2)^{-1}\).

marking_criteria.description_html:

Keep the factor 3 when integrating \((3t\pm2)^{-1}\).

questions.title: A half-angle factor and a minimum
questions.prompt_html:
For \(0\lt \theta\lt \pi\),

\[\sin{\left(\theta \right)}\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d \theta} +y=3 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}\]

and \(y(\pi/2)=2\).

  1. Find the particular solution.

    [7]

  2. Find the minimum value of \(y\) and the value of \(\theta\) where it occurs.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{3 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{2 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}}\]

(b)

\[y_{\min}=\sqrt3,\qquad \theta=\frac\pi3.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Divide by \(\sin\theta\). Since \(0\lt \theta\lt \pi\), an integrating factor is

\[\mu=\exp\!\left(\int\operatorname{cosec}\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\right)=\tan\frac\theta2.\]
\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\theta}\left(y\tan\frac\theta2\right)=\frac32\tan\frac\theta2\sec^2\frac\theta2.\]

Put \(u=\tan(\theta/2)\). Then \(du=\tfrac12\sec^2(\theta/2)\,d\theta\), so the integral is \(\tfrac32u^2\).

\[y\tan\frac\theta2=\frac32\tan^2\frac\theta2+C.\]

The condition \(y(\pi/2)=2\) gives \(C=1/2\).

\[y=\frac{3 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{2 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}}.\]

(b)

Put \(u=\tan(\theta/2)\gt 0\). Then \(y=3u/2+1/(2u)\). Differentiating with respect to \(u\) gives \(3/2-1/(2u^2)=0\), hence \(u=1/\sqrt3\). The expression tends to infinity at both ends and has positive second derivative \(u^{-3}\). Thus the unique minimum is \(\sqrt3\) at \(\theta=\pi/3\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\int\operatorname{cosec}\theta\,d\theta=\ln\tan(\theta/2)\) on this interval.

(b)

Minimise as a function of the positive half-angle tangent.

marking_criteria.description_html:

Method and reasoning:

questions.title: Conjugate radicals and a finite limit
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\gt 2\),

\[\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +y=x \left(x - \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}\right)\]

and \(y(5/2)=2\).

  1. Show that \(x+\sqrt{x^2-4}\) is an integrating factor in standard linear form.

    [3]

  2. Hence find \(y\) explicitly.

    [6]

  3. Find \(\lim_{x\to\infty}y\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mu=x+\sqrt{x^2-4}.\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{4 \sqrt{x^{2} - 4} + 2}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}\]

(c)

\[\lim_{x\to\infty}y=2.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

After dividing by \(r=\sqrt{x^2-4}\), the coefficient is \(1/r\). Also \(\mu^\prime=1+x/r=(x+r)/r=\mu/r\).

(b)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}\,y=\frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}} - x\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}\,\mathrm d x\right)=x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\frac{4 x}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}.\]

The key simplification is \((x+r)(x-r)=4\), where \(r=\sqrt{x^2-4}\). Therefore the multiplied right side is \(4x/r\).

\[\mu y=4 \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[8=6+C,\qquad C=2.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{4 \sqrt{x^{2} - 4} + 2}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}.\]

(c)

Divide numerator and denominator of \(y=(4r+2)/(x+r)\) by \(x\). Since \(r/x\to1\), the limit is \(4/(1+1)=2\).

(a)

Check the logarithmic derivative of the proposed factor.

(b)

Multiply the conjugate radical factors before integrating.

(c)

Do not drop the square-root term from the denominator.

questions.title: A radical factor with two zero crossings
questions.prompt_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\left(x^{2} + 4\right)\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\,y=x \left(x - \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\right)\]

with \(y(0)=\ln3\).

  1. Show that \(x+\sqrt{x^2+4}\) is an integrating factor in linear form.

    [4]

  2. Find the particular solution.

    [5]

  3. Find all real zeros of the solution.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mu=x+\sqrt{x^2+4}.\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{2 \ln{\left(\frac{12}{x^{2} + 4} \right)}}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}}\]

(c)

\[x=\pm2\sqrt2.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The standard coefficient is \(P=(x^2+4)^{-1/2}\). Hence \(\int P\,dx=\sinh^{-1}(x/2)\). Exponentiation gives \((x+\sqrt{x^2+4})/2\); multiplying by 2 produces the stated factor.

(b)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}}\,y=\frac{x \left(x - \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\right)}{x^{2} + 4}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}}\,\mathrm d x\right)=x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=- \frac{4 x}{x^{2} + 4}.\]

Combine the logarithms to obtain

\[y=\frac{2 \ln{\left(\frac{12}{x^{2} + 4} \right)}}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}}.\]

questions.title: A polynomial times an exponential
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\gt 0\),

\[x\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +2\,y=x e^{2 x}\]

and \(y(1)=1\).

  1. Find the particular solution.

    [7]

  2. Find \(\lim_{x\to\infty}y e^{-2x}\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\right) e^{2 x} - \frac{e^{2}}{4} + 1}{x^{2}}\]

(b)

\[\lim_{x\to\infty}y e^{-2x}=\frac12.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{2}{x}\,y=e^{2 x}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{2}{x}\,\mathrm d x\right)=x^{2}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=x^{2} e^{2 x}.\]

Two integrations by parts give

\[\int x^2e^{2x}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{x^2e^{2x}}2-\int xe^{2x}\,\mathrm dx=e^{2x}\left(\frac{x^2}2-\frac x2+\frac14\right).\]
\[\mu y=\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\right) e^{2 x}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[1=\frac{e^{2}}{4}+C,\qquad C=1 - \frac{e^{2}}{4}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\right) e^{2 x} - \frac{e^{2}}{4} + 1}{x^{2}}.\]

(b)

Divide the explicit expression by \(e^{2x}\). The remaining nonconstant terms are multiples of \(x^{-1},x^{-2},x^{-2}e^{-2x}\), all of which tend to zero.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

After using \(\mu=x^2\), integrate \(x^2e^{2x}\) by parts twice.

(b)

Simplify the ratio rather than trying to subtract two divergent expressions.

\[y=\frac{\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\right) e^{2 x} - \frac{e^{2}}{4} + 1}{x^{2}}\]

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{6 x}{3 x^{2} + 2}\,y=x^{2}\]

questions.title: Integrating an inverse sine inside a linear equation
questions.prompt_html:
Use \(0\lt x\lt 4\) throughout.

  1. Use \(u=4-(x-2)^2\) to find \(\int (x-2)/\sqrt{4-(x-2)^2}\,dx\).

    [3]

  2. Find the solution of

    \[xy^\prime-y=x^2\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{2}\right)\]

    with \(y(2)=3\).

    [9]

  3. Find \(\lim_{x\to4^-}y\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\int\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{4-(x-2)^2}}\,\mathrm dx=-\sqrt{4-(x-2)^2}+C.\]

(b)

\[y=x \left(\sqrt{4 - \left(x - 2\right)^{2}} + \left(x - 2\right) \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)} - \frac{1}{2}\right)\]

(c)

\[\lim_{x\to4^-}y=4\pi-2.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The substitution gives \(du=-2(x-2)dx\). The integral becomes \(-\tfrac12\int u^{-1/2}du=-\sqrt u+C\). Substitute back.

(b)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{1}{x}\,y=x \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int - \frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm d x\right)=\frac{1}{x}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)}.\]

Integration by parts, with \(w=\sin^{-1}((x-2)/2)\) and \(dv=dx\), is most conveniently written using the shifted factor \(x-2\):

\[\int\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{2}\right)\,\mathrm dx=(x-2)\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{2}\right)-\int\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{4-(x-2)^2}}\,\mathrm dx.\]
\[\mu y=\sqrt{4 - \left(x - 2\right)^{2}} + \left(x - 2\right) \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[\frac{3}{2}=2+C,\qquad C=- \frac{1}{2}.\]

Therefore

\[y=x \left(\sqrt{4 - \left(x - 2\right)^{2}} + \left(x - 2\right) \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)} - \frac{1}{2}\right).\]

(c)

As \(x\to4^-\), the inverse sine tends to \(\pi/2\) and the square-root term tends to zero. Thus \(y\to4(2\cdot\pi/2-1/2)=4\pi-2\). The endpoint is a one-sided limit on the stated domain.

(a)

Keep the negative sign from the substitution.

(b)

An integrating factor is \(1/x\). Use integration by parts and then part (a).

(c)

Use the branch \(-\pi/2\le\sin^{-1}u\le\pi/2\).

questions.title: Salt concentration in a well-mixed tank
questions.prompt_html:
A tank contains 30 litres of liquid and initially no salt. Brine containing 3 grams of salt per litre enters at 2 litres per minute. The well-mixed liquid leaves at the same rate. Let \(S(t)\) be the mass of salt, in grams, after \(t\) minutes. Assume constant flow rates and instantaneous mixing.

  1. Form a differential equation for \(S\).

    [2]

  2. Solve the equation and give the concentration as a function of \(t\).

    [5]

  3. Find the first time at which the concentration reaches 2 grams per litre.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dt}=6-\frac{S}{15},\qquad S(0)=0.\]

(b)

\[S=90(1-e^{-t/15}),\qquad c=3(1-e^{-t/15})\ \mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}.\]

(c)

\[t=15\ln3\ \text{minutes}.\]

(a)

The inflow adds \(2\times3=6\) grams per minute. The concentration inside the tank is \(S/30\) grams per litre, so the outflow removes \(2S/30=S/15\) grams per minute. Subtract removal from input.

(b)

The integrating factor is \(e^{t/15}\).

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(Se^{t/15})=6e^{t/15},\qquad Se^{t/15}=90e^{t/15}+C.\]

Since \(S(0)=0\), \(C=-90\). Divide by \(e^{t/15}\) and then by the tank volume 30 to obtain the concentration.

(c)

\(3(1-e^{-t/15})=2\) gives \(e^{-t/15}=1/3\). The concentration is strictly increasing for \(t\ge0\), so this is the unique first crossing.

Use mass rate in minus mass rate out, not concentration rate directly.

(b)

The mass and the concentration differ by the fixed factor 30.

(c)

Use the concentration formula, not \(S=2\).

questions.title: Inferring an equilibrium level from three observations
questions.prompt_html:
A measured response \(T(t)\) follows the model

\[\frac{\mathrm dT}{\mathrm dt}=-k(T-A),\qquad k\gt 0,\]

where \(A\) and \(k\) are constants. Exact observations are \(T(0)=20\), \(T(2)=12\) and \(T(4)=8\).

  1. Solve the equation in terms of \(A\) and \(k\), using \(T(0)=20\).

    [3]

  2. Use the other two observations to determine \(A\) and \(k\).

    [3]

  3. Find the first time when \(T=6\) and state the limiting response.

    [2]

(a)

\[T=A+(20-A)e^{-kt}.\]

(b)

(c)

(b)

The decreases over equal time intervals form a geometric sequence.

(c)

questions.prompt_html:
For \(t\ge0\), the response \(y\) satisfies

\[y^{\prime\prime}+6y^\prime+13y=90\cos t.\]

  1. Find the general solution.

    [6]

  2. Find the solution with \(y(0)=4\) and \(y^\prime(0)=0\).

    [4]

  3. Show that every solution is asymptotic, in the sense of a vanishing difference, to \(R\cos(t-\phi)\). Determine \(R\) and \(\phi\) exactly, with \(0\lt \phi\lt \pi/2\). State whether \(y\) has a limit.

    [4]

(a)

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

(b)

\[y=3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)} - \frac{9 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} - 2 e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\]

(c)

\[R=3\sqrt5,\qquad \phi=\tan^{-1}\!\frac12.\]

There is no pointwise limit.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation is

\[m^{2} + 6 m + 13=0,\qquad m=-3\pm 2i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Try a particular integral containing both sine and cosine:

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a \cos{\left(t \right)} + b \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives

\[\begin{aligned}12 a + 6 b - 90 = 0\\- 6 a + 12 b = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=6,\qquad b=3.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

Add the complementary function and particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

(b)

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- 2 C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 3 C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} - 3 C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} - 6 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = -2\\- 3 C_{1} + 2 C_{2} = -3\end{aligned}\]

questions.prompt_html:

\[y^{\prime\prime}-y^\prime-6y=5e^{-2x}.\]

(b)

(a)

questions.title: A reciprocal solution with a provably positive denominator
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\ge0\), a nonzero function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{2(y^\prime)^2}{y^3}-\frac{y^{\prime\prime}}{y^2}-\frac{4y^\prime}{y^2}+\frac8y=8x^2+14,\]

with \(y(0)=1/3\) and \(y^\prime(0)=1/9\).

  1. Use \(v=1/y\) to show that \(v^{\prime\prime}+4v^\prime+8v=8x^2+14\).

    [4]

  2. Hence find the required solution for \(y\).

    [8]

  3. Show that the denominator of your expression is positive for every \(x\ge0\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 v}{\mathrm d x^2} +4\,\frac{\mathrm d v}{\mathrm d x} +8\,v=8 x^{2} + 14\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{1}{x^{2} - x + 2 + e^{- 2 x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + e^{- 2 x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}\]

(c)

\[v\ge\frac74-\sqrt2\gt 0.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[v^\prime=-\frac{y^\prime}{y^2},\qquad v^{\prime\prime}=\frac{2(y^\prime)^2}{y^3}-\frac{y^{\prime\prime}}{y^2}.\]

Substitute these two derivatives and \(v=1/y\) into the left side to obtain the required linear equation.

(b)

The transformed initial values are \(v(0)=3\) and \(v^\prime(0)=-(1/9)/(1/3)^2=-1\).

The auxiliary equation is

\[m^{2} + 4 m + 8=0,\qquad m=-2\pm 2i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[v_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 2 x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 2 x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)}.\]

For a polynomial particular integral, try

\[v_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} x + a_{2} x^{2}.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}8 a_{2} - 8 = 0\\8 a_{1} + 8 a_{2} = 0\\8 a_{0} + 4 a_{1} + 2 a_{2} - 14 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=2,\quad a_{1}=-1,\quad a_{2}=1\]
\[v_{\mathrm{PI}}=x^{2} - x + 2.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[v=C_{1} e^{- 2 x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 2 x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + x^{2} - x + 2.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[v^\prime=- 2 C_{1} e^{- 2 x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)} - 2 C_{1} e^{- 2 x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)} - 2 C_{2} e^{- 2 x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 2 C_{2} e^{- 2 x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + 2 x - 1.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = 1\\- 2 C_{1} + 2 C_{2} = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=1,\qquad C_2=1.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[v=x^{2} - x + 2 + e^{- 2 x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + e^{- 2 x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)}.\]

Take the reciprocal:

\[y=\frac{1}{x^{2} - x + 2 + e^{- 2 x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + e^{- 2 x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}.\]

(c)

\(x^2-x+2=(x-1/2)^2+7/4\ge7/4\). Also \(|e^{-2x}(\cos2x+\sin2x)|\le\sqrt2\) for \(x\ge0\). Combining these gives the positive lower bound, so the reciprocal solution has no singularity on the stated interval.

Work on \(t\gt 0\). The function \(y\) satisfies

\[t\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +2\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +4 t\,y=4 t^{2} + 6\]

At \(t=\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(y=\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=1 + \frac{4}{\pi}\).

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 v}{\mathrm d t^2} +4\,v=4 t^{2} + 6\]

(b)

\[v^\prime=- 2 C_{1} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 C_{2} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 t.\]

questions.title: A fourth-power substitution without a hidden branch change
questions.prompt_html:
A positive function \(y\) satisfies

\[y^3y^{\prime\prime}+3y^2(y^\prime)^2+2y^3y^\prime+\frac54y^4=\frac32e^{-x},\]

with \(y(0)=1\) and \(y^\prime(0)=-1/4\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(y\) as an explicit function of \(x\).

    [8]

    [2]

(a)

\[v^{\prime\prime}+2v^\prime+5v=6e^{-x}.\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{2^{\frac{3}{4}} \sqrt[4]{3 - \cos{\left(2 x \right)}} e^{- \frac{x}{4}}}{2}\]

(c)

It is defined and positive for every real \(x\) and tends to zero as \(x\to\infty\).

(a)

\[v^\prime=4y^3y^\prime,\qquad v^{\prime\prime}=12y^2(y^\prime)^2+4y^3y^{\prime\prime}.\]

Multiplying the original equation by 4 groups its terms into \(v^{\prime\prime}+2v^\prime+5v\).

(b)

The initial data become \(v(0)=1\) and \(v^\prime(0)=4(1)^3(-1/4)=-1\).

The auxiliary equation is

\[m^{2} + 2 m + 5=0,\qquad m=-1\pm 2i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[v_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + C_{2} e^{- x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)}.\]

Try \(v_{\mathrm{PI}}=K e^{- x}\). Substitution gives

\[4 K=6,\qquad K=\frac{3}{2}.\]
\[v_{\mathrm{PI}}=\frac{3 e^{- x}}{2}.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[v=C_{1} e^{- x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + C_{2} e^{- x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + \frac{3 e^{- x}}{2}.\]

\[v^\prime=- 2 C_{1} e^{- x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)} - C_{1} e^{- x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)} - C_{2} e^{- x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 2 C_{2} e^{- x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)} - \frac{3 e^{- x}}{2}.\]

\[C_1=- \frac{1}{2},\qquad C_2=0.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[v=- \frac{e^{- x} \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2} + \frac{3 e^{- x}}{2}.\]

\[y=\frac{2^{\frac{3}{4}} \sqrt[4]{3 - \cos{\left(2 x \right)}} e^{- \frac{x}{4}}}{2}.\]

\(1\le(3-\cos2x)/2\le2\), so the radicand lies between \(e^{-x}\) and \(2e^{-x}\). It is therefore positive for every real \(x\) and tends to zero for large positive \(x\). Taking positive fourth roots proves the conclusion.

    [6]

\[v^{\prime\prime}-v^\prime-6v=12e^{2x}.\]

(b)

\[y=\sqrt[3]{C_{1} e^{3 x} + C_{2} e^{- 2 x} - 3 e^{2 x}},\]

where the cube root is real, on any interval where its argument is nonzero.

(c)

At \(y=0\) its left side would be zero, but its right side is strictly positive.

(a)

\[v^\prime=3y^2y^\prime,\qquad v^{\prime\prime}=6y(y^\prime)^2+3y^2y^{\prime\prime}.\]

\[y=\sqrt[3]{C_{1} e^{3 x} + C_{2} e^{- 2 x} - 3 e^{2 x}},\]

(a)

On an interval where \(y\ne0\), \(v^\prime=-y^\prime/y^2\). Divide the original equation by \(y^2\) and substitute to obtain \(-v^\prime+2v=3\).

(b)

For \(v^\prime-2v=-3\), an integrating factor is \(e^{-2x}\).

\[(ve^{-2x})^\prime=-3e^{-2x},\qquad v=\frac32+Ce^{2x}.\]

The initial value is \(v(0)=2\), so \(C=1/2\). Taking the reciprocal gives

\[y=\frac{2}{e^{2 x} + 3}.\]

(c)

The denominator \(3+e^{2x}\) is strictly positive. It tends to infinity as \(x\to\infty\), proving the stated limit. The separately possible solution \(y\equiv0\) does not satisfy the given initial condition.

questions.title: An Euler-type equation with logarithmic forcing
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\gt 0\),

\[x^2y^{\prime\prime}+5xy^\prime+13y=26\ln x-5,\]

with \(y(1)=0\) and \(y^\prime(1)=1\).

  1. With \(x=e^u\), show that \(xy^\prime=dy/du\) and \(x^2y^{\prime\prime}=d^2y/du^2-dy/du\).

    [3]

  2. Deduce the transformed equation for \(y\) as a function of \(u\).

    [2]

  3. Find the required solution in terms of \(x\).

    [8]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[xy_x=y_u,\qquad x^2y_{xx}=y_{uu}-y_u.\]

(b)

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d u^2} +4\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d u} +13\,y=26 u - 5\]

(c)

\[y=2 \ln{\left(x \right)} - 1 + \frac{\sin{\left(3 \ln{\left(x \right)} \right)}}{3 x^{2}} + \frac{\cos{\left(3 \ln{\left(x \right)} \right)}}{x^{2}}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(du/dx=1/x\), \(y_x=y_u/x\). Differentiating once more gives \(y_{xx}=y_{uu}/x^2-y_u/x^2\).

(b)

Substitute the two derivative identities and \(\ln x=u\). The first-derivative coefficient becomes \(-1+5=4\).

(c)

At \(x=1\) we have \(u=0\), \(y=0\) and \(y_u=xy_x=1\).

The auxiliary equation is

\[m^{2} + 4 m + 13=0,\qquad m=-2\pm 3i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 2 u} \cos{\left(3 u \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 2 u} \sin{\left(3 u \right)}.\]

For a polynomial particular integral, try

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} u.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}13 a_{1} - 26 = 0\\13 a_{0} + 4 a_{1} + 5 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=-1,\quad a_{1}=2\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=2 u - 1.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 u} \cos{\left(3 u \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 2 u} \sin{\left(3 u \right)} + 2 u - 1.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- 3 C_{1} e^{- 2 u} \sin{\left(3 u \right)} - 2 C_{1} e^{- 2 u} \cos{\left(3 u \right)} - 2 C_{2} e^{- 2 u} \sin{\left(3 u \right)} + 3 C_{2} e^{- 2 u} \cos{\left(3 u \right)} + 2.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = 1\\- 2 C_{1} + 3 C_{2} = -1\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=1,\qquad C_2=\frac{1}{3}.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=2 u - 1 + \frac{e^{- 2 u} \sin{\left(3 u \right)}}{3} + e^{- 2 u} \cos{\left(3 u \right)}.\]

Return to \(u=\ln x\) and \(e^{-2u}=x^{-2}\):

\[y=2 \ln{\left(x \right)} - 1 + \frac{\sin{\left(3 \ln{\left(x \right)} \right)}}{3 x^{2}} + \frac{\cos{\left(3 \ln{\left(x \right)} \right)}}{x^{2}}.\]

(b)

(c)

Translate the derivative initial condition using \(y_u=xy_x\).

questions.title: A translated combination that becomes separable
questions.prompt_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{x+2y+3}{2(x+2y-1)},\qquad y(0)=1.\]

  1. Use \(z=x+2y\) to find the solution in implicit form. Use the branch through the initial point.

    [7]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac x2-y+\ln\!\left(\frac{x+2y+1}{3}\right)+1=0,\qquad x+2y\gt 1.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate \(z=x+2y\):

\[\frac{\mathrm dz}{\mathrm dx}=1+2\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=1+\frac{z+3}{z-1}=\frac{2(z+1)}{z-1}.\]

Near the initial value \(z(0)=2\), we have \(z\gt 1\). Separate variables:

\[\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dz}=\frac{z-1}{2(z+1)}=\frac12-\frac1{z+1}.\]
\[x=\frac z2-\ln(z+1)+C.\]

At \(x=0,z=2\), \(C=\ln3-1\). Substitute \(z=x+2y\) and rearrange to obtain the stated implicit equation. The logarithm is positive in its argument because \(z\gt 1\). The constant solution \(z=-1\), excluded when separating, does not satisfy the initial condition.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The derivative of the new variable is \(1+2y^\prime\), not simply \(y^\prime\).

questions.title: A homogeneous substitution and the sign of a square root
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x\gt 0\),

\[xy^\prime=y+2\sqrt{4x^2+y^2},\qquad y(1)=0.\]

  1. Use \(y=vx\) to find the particular solution explicitly.

    [8]

  2. Determine where the solution is positive, zero or negative on its domain.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=x^3-\frac1x,\qquad x\gt 0.\]

(b)

\[y\lt 0\ (0\lt x\lt 1),\qquad y=0\ (x=1),\qquad y\gt 0\ (x\gt 1).\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The substitution gives \(y^\prime=v+xv^\prime\). Because \(x\gt 0\),

\[\sqrt{4x^2+y^2}=x\sqrt{4+v^2}.\]

The terms \(xv\) cancel, leaving

\[x\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=2\sqrt{4+v^2}.\]

Separate and integrate:

\[\sinh^{-1}\!\frac v2=2\ln x+C.\]

At \(x=1\), \(v=y/x=0\), hence \(C=0\). Therefore

\[v=2\sinh(2\ln x)=e^{2\ln x}-e^{-2\ln x}=x^2-x^{-2}.\]

Multiplication by \(x\) gives the required solution.

(b)

Write \(y=(x^4-1)/x\). Since \(x\gt 0\), its sign is the sign of \(x^4-1\). The only positive zero is 1.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\sqrt{x^2}=|x|\) before using the stipulated sign of \(x\).

(b)

Do not add the root \(x=-1\) to a domain restricted to positive \(x\).

Method and reasoning:
